ai.literal: Having known the nature, before a capable assembly, will not slip in speech, those of purity who have known the collection of words.
ai.translation: Those of pure mind who know the arrangement of words will not falter in their speech before a powerful assembly, once they have understood its nature.
ai.modern: அவையின் தன்மையை அறிந்து, சொற்களின் தொகுதியை உணர்ந்த தூய்மையான அறிவை உடையவர்கள், வல்லமை மிக்க அவையின் முன் பேசும்போது வாய் தவறிப் பிழை செய்ய மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains how a speaker can address an audience without fear or error. Those who possess a pure, flawless intellect and a deep mastery over vocabulary ('colliṉ tokai') will never falter or make slips of the tongue ('vāy cōrār'). By first analyzing and understanding the specific nature of the audience ('vakai aṟintu'), they can confidently deliver their speech even before a highly capable and powerful assembly ('val avai').

ai.literal: Among the learned, the learned they will be called, who before the learned, what they learned, so as to enter their minds, speak.
ai.translation: Those who can speak what they have learned in such a way that it deeply enters the minds of the learned assembled before them, will be regarded as the most learned among the learned.
ai.modern: கற்றறிந்த அறிஞர்களின் முன்னிலையில், தாம் கற்றவற்றை அவர்களின் மனதில் பதியும்படி எடுத்துச் சொல்ல வல்லவர்கள், கற்றவர்களுக்கெல்லாம் கற்றவர் என்று போற்றப்படுவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes that true scholarship is validated only when it can be communicated effectively to other scholars. The word 'செல' literally means 'to go' or 'to enter', which in this context means making one's ideas penetrate and be accepted by the minds of the audience. It is not enough to merely possess knowledge; one must have the courage and skill to articulate it clearly before an assembly of experts. Those who can successfully convey their learning to other learned people are crowned as the best among scholars.

ai.literal: In the midst of battle, those who die are easy to find; rare are those who do not fear in the midst of an assembly.
ai.translation: Those who can face death in the midst of battle are easy to find; but those who can stand without fear in the midst of an assembly are truly rare.
ai.modern: போர்க்களத்தில் சாகக்கூடியவர்கள் எளிதாகக் கிடைப்பார்கள்; ஆனால் அவையின் நடுவே அச்சமின்றிப் பேசக்கூடியவர்கள் கிடைப்பது அரிது.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts physical bravery in battle with intellectual courage in a public assembly. The author notes that many soldiers are willing to face death on the battlefield, making such brave individuals relatively common. However, standing before a learned assembly without fear requires a different, rarer kind of courage. The key words 'பகை' (battle) and 'அவை' (assembly) represent two different arenas of human trial, highlighting that mental fortitude before peers is scarcer than physical valor.

ai.literal: Before the learned, speaking what was learned so as to penetrate (their minds), and from those who are superior (in learning), acquiring their superior knowledge.
ai.translation: Speak what you have learned before the learned so that it deeply penetrates their minds; and from those who are more learned than yourself, acquire their superior knowledge.
ai.modern: கற்றவர்களின் முன்னே தான் கற்றவற்றை அவர்கள் மனதில் பதியுமாறு சொல்லி, தன்னைவிட அறிவில் சிறந்தவர்களிடமிருந்து அவர்கள் கற்ற சிறந்த அறிவைப் பெற்றுக்கொள்ள வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet outlines the dual duty of a scholar when interacting with an assembly of the learned. First, one must present what they have learned in a clear, convincing manner so that it is accepted and understood by other scholars. Second, one must remain open to learning, actively acquiring the deeper, superior knowledge possessed by those who are even more learned. This approach ensures both the effective sharing of one's own knowledge and the continuous growth of one's intellect without fear or arrogance.

ai.literal: According to the systematic path, the measure having known, one should learn, for the sake of giving a reply without fearing the assembly.
ai.translation: One should study systematically, knowing the measure of what is to be learned, for the purpose of giving a fearless reply in an assembly.
ai.modern: அவைக்கு அஞ்சாமல் பதில் கூறுவதற்காக, முறையான வழியில் நூல்களின் எல்லையை அறிந்து கற்க வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights how systematic learning builds the confidence needed for public speaking. To speak without fear in an assembly, one must learn by understanding the proper method and scope of the subjects. Knowing the limits and depth of knowledge prevents hesitation and errors when answering others. Thus, structured learning is presented as the foundation of fearless communication.

ai.literal: With a sword, what use is there to those who are not brave? With books of learning, what use is there to those who fear the subtle assembly?
ai.translation: What is the use of a sword to those who lack courage? Likewise, what is the use of learned treatises to those who fear to speak before an assembly of refined minds?
ai.modern: துணிவில்லாதவர்களுக்குக் கையில் இருக்கும் வாளினால் என்ன பயன்? அதுபோல, நுட்பமான அறிவை உடையவர்களின் அவையைக் கண்டு அஞ்சுபவர்களுக்கு அவர்கள் கற்ற நூல்களினால் என்ன பயன்?
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a vivid analogy to highlight the futility of learning without the courage to present it. Just as a sword is completely useless in the hands of a coward who lacks the bravery to fight, learned books and treatises are of no value to someone who trembles with fear before an assembly of refined, intelligent people. The word 'vaṉkaṇṇar' refers to those with courage or strength of mind, and 'nuṇ avai' refers to an assembly of subtle, sharp intellects. The poet emphasizes that courage is essential to make one's education meaningful and impactful in public life.

ai.literal: Inside the battlefield, a coward's hand bright sword, inside the assembly, he who fears, his learned book.
ai.translation: The learning of one who fears to face an assembly is like a bright sword in the hand of a coward on a battlefield.
ai.modern: போர்க்களத்தில் பேடியின் கையில் இருக்கும் கூர்மையான வாளைப் போன்றது, அவைக்கு அஞ்சுகின்றவன் கற்ற நூல் அறிவு.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses a vivid analogy to show the uselessness of education without courage. A bright, sharp sword (ஒள்வாள்) is a powerful weapon, but it is completely useless in the hand of a coward (பேடிகை) on a battlefield. Similarly, the books and treatises learned (கற்ற நூல்) by a person are of no value if that person is terrified of speaking before an assembly (அவையகத்து அஞ்சுமவன்). True learning requires the courage of expression to be of any practical use.

ai.literal: Many subjects even though having learned, benefit they indeed do not have, in a good assembly, well so as to be received, those who do not speak.
ai.translation: Even though they have learned many subjects, those who cannot speak in a way that penetrates the minds of a good assembly are of no use at all.
ai.modern: நல்ல சபையிலே கேட்பவர் மனதில் பதியும்படி நன்றாக எடுத்துச் சொல்லத் தெரியாதவர்கள், பல நூல்களைக் கற்றிருந்தாலும் அதனால் ஒரு பயனும் இல்லாதவர்களே ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes that the ultimate test of learning is the ability to communicate it effectively to others. The word 'பல்லவை' refers to many diverse subjects of study, and 'செல' means to penetrate or go deep into the minds of the listeners. Those who fail to speak clearly and convincingly before a good assembly ('நல்லவையுள்') render all their extensive education useless ('பயமிலரே'). True knowledge must be accompanied by the courage and skill to articulate it, otherwise, it remains locked away and serves no purpose.

ai.literal: Than those who have not learned, the lowest, they say, [are those who] having learned and known, fear the assembly of the good.
ai.translation: They say that those who fear to face an assembly of the wise, even though they have studied and acquired knowledge, are worse than the unlearned.
ai.modern: கற்றுக்கொண்டு எல்லாவற்றையும் அறிந்திருந்தாலும், நல்லவர்களுடைய அவைக்கு அஞ்சுபவர்களை, கல்லாதவர்களை விடக் கடைசியானவர்கள் என்று கூறுவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the futility of education without the courage to speak before an audience. The author states that people who have studied deeply and acquired vast knowledge, yet tremble with fear when facing an assembly of wise and good people, are considered inferior even to those who are completely uneducated. The key words 'கற்று அறிந்தும்' (even though having learned and known) contrast sharply with 'கல்லாதவரின் கடை' (lower than the unlearned), emphasizing that knowledge is useless if it cannot be expressed confidently in public. The term 'நல்லார் அவை' refers to an assembly of noble or learned people, which is the ultimate testing ground for one's learning.

ai.literal: Even though they are alive, they are equal to those who do not exist—those who, fearing the assembly, do not speak what they have learned so that it penetrates.
ai.translation: Though they are alive, those who fear the assembly and fail to speak what they have learned in a way that penetrates the minds of others are equal to the dead.
ai.modern: அவைக்கு அஞ்சி, தாம் கற்றவற்றை கேட்பவர் மனதில் பதியுமாறு சொல்ல முடியாதவர்கள், உயிரோடு வாழ்ந்தாலும் இறந்தவர்களுக்கு ஒப்பாவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the uselessness of education when paired with cowardice. The poet argues that those who fear the assembly (களன் அஞ்சி) and fail to present their knowledge in an impactful, convincing manner (செலச் சொல்லாதார்) are practically useless to society. Even though they are physically alive (உளர் எனினும்), their silence makes them equivalent to the dead or non-existent (இல்லாரொடு ஒப்பர்). Thus, the courage to speak in public is as essential as the acquisition of knowledge itself.
